Reverse-mortgage cash at closing: deduct old debt and fees before budgeting the advance

Reconcile net cash after fees and an old mortgage payout, follow hypothetical capitalized interest and inspect a property-sale remainder before contractual protections.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Follow an upfront advance, accumulated interest and a separate property scenario

Interactive planning lab

Advance less fees and old-debt settlement$156,000
Modeled loan balance before contract protections$569,789.35
Sale remainder before contract protections$399,235.86

Hypothetical arithmetic, not a reverse-mortgage offer, approval, property appraisal or actual payout quote. One initial gross advance is borrowed; entered upfront costs and the listed old-debt payout are deducted from its proceeds and are not added to the new debt again. No further borrowing or regular repayments occur. The constant nominal annual rate is divided by 12 and interest capitalizes monthly; actual contract rates and compounding may differ. Home value changes at an independent assumed annual rate, and selling costs are a percentage of the modeled sale value. The debt balance is deliberately uncapped. A negative raw property remainder is an arithmetic gap before contractual protections, not a finding of personal or estate liability. No lender guarantee is calculated. Taxes, property upkeep, insurance, accrued post-due interest, other liens and the use of the cash advance are excluded.

The central idea

Read the usable cash, growing loan balance and property scenario together. A future arithmetic gap is not a calculation of the liability payable under an actual reverse-mortgage contract.

01

Start with the cash that remains after the initial deductions

A reverse mortgage is a loan secured against home equity. The FCAC’s consumer guide describes it for homeowners usually aged fifty-five or older, with eligibility and borrowing amounts depending on the property, owners and lender. These charts do not calculate that eligibility.

The first figure starts with a fictional CAD 200,000 gross advance. It deducts CAD 4,000 of upfront costs and CAD 40,000 required to settle an existing secured loan. The result is CAD 156,000 of cash available from this particular funding arrangement.

The new debt starts at CAD 200,000. It does not start at CAD 156,000, and the model does not add the fees or old payout to the gross advance again. The deductions explain how the borrowed money is used. If they exceed the advance, the chart shows an initial cash requirement that needs another source; it does not increase approved borrowing automatically.

02

Follow interest added to the balance

For this illustration, the nominal annual rate stays at 7%, divided by twelve, and no regular payment or further advance occurs. Each month, interest is added to the modeled balance. The formula after m months is 200,000 × (1 + 0.07/12)m.

After fifteen years, the calculated balance is about CAD 569,789.35. Of that amount, CAD 200,000 is the original gross advance and CAD 369,789.35 is accumulated interest. The stacked chart keeps those two components visible over independent elapsed-time scenarios.

The interest grows with the balance on which it is charged. It is therefore different from multiplying the original amount by 7% and fifteen years. Monthly capitalization is an explicit teaching convention here, rather than a claim about every lender’s contract. A real rate can change, compounding can differ and additional advances or repayments would alter the path.

03

Give the property its own assumption

The home starts at a hypothetical CAD 750,000. With the selected 2% annual value increase, its modeled value after fifteen years is CAD 1,009,401.25. That calculation is independent of the loan’s interest rate.

The second chart places home value beside the loan balance. The property is an asset; its assumed appreciation does not itself make a cash payment to the lender. A different value path can leave more or less equity even when the advance and interest terms are unchanged.

The smooth line is not a property appraisal, an observed house-price series or a forecast for a neighbourhood. The model also excludes upkeep, insurance, property taxes and the way the household uses its advance. It cannot establish the complete cost of staying in the home or the change in total household wealth.

04

Reconcile a sale before interpreting the remainder

At the selected fifteen-year date, assumed selling costs of 4% reduce the CAD 1,009,401.25 modeled sale value by about CAD 40,376.05. That leaves CAD 969,025.20 before settling the loan in this partial reconciliation.

Subtracting the uncapped calculated balance of CAD 569,789.35 gives a raw property remainder of about CAD 399,235.86. The fourth figure displays those steps. It excludes other claims, actual closing adjustments, taxes and any contractual repayment charge.

This property-only remainder does not add back the initial CAD 156,000 of net proceeds. That money may have been spent, retained or used for another purpose, none of which is tracked here. Counting it as an asset at the future date would require a separate cash and investment ledger.

05

Treat a negative cell as arithmetic before contract protections

The final grid changes the constant loan rate and annual home-value assumption independently while preserving the selected gross advance, horizon and selling-cost percentage. Negative cells mean that modeled net sale value is below the uncapped mathematical balance.

That difference does not establish that a borrower or estate must pay the shortfall from other assets. For a specifically attributed example, HomeEquity Bank describes a conditional No Negative Equity Guarantee for CHIP. Its stated conditions include maintaining the property, paying property taxes and insurance, and meeting mortgage obligations. It excludes administrative expenses and interest accumulated after the due date.

The chart does not reproduce that guarantee or extend it to every product. Simply replacing debt with the smaller of the calculated balance and the modeled sale value would also fail to represent all of those conditions. Actual protections, valuation terms, sale costs, obligations and repayment dates need the signed contract and a lender statement.

06

Put the repayment event and household obligations on a calendar

The FCAC’s home-equity borrowing overview identifies sale, moving out, the last borrower’s death and default as repayment events for a reverse mortgage. The actual timing and consequences depend on the agreement. The selected sale year is only a scenario; it is not permission to leave the balance outstanding until that date.

Retaining ownership comes with ongoing costs and contractual responsibilities. The absence of a regular mortgage payment in these charts does not fund property taxes, repairs, insurance or a later move. Those obligations belong in the household cash budget alongside any use of the advance.

An estate may also face a repayment deadline before every other administrative step is complete. The graphs calculate neither estate administration nor a bridge facility. Record the relevant repayment trigger, required evidence, settlement window and other housing commitments separately from the interest calculation.

07

Bring the complete quote back to the planning question

A reviewable quote needs the approved gross advance, any existing secured-debt payout, itemized fees, net proceeds, rate and compounding method, future-advance terms, repayment conditions and available protections. Confirm how any guarantee treats property obligations, due dates and excluded amounts.

The personal planning question then needs its own dates and dollars. How much usable cash is required, when is it needed, what recurring housing costs continue, and what cash would be available if the household moves earlier? The model’s one-advance structure cannot answer a plan that needs later borrowing without adding those future cash flows.

Keep the fictional sensitivities as a way to inspect the mechanics. Compare actual alternatives with matched cash needs, expenses and ending assets and debts. Neither a large initial advance nor a positive modeled property remainder alone determines whether a reverse mortgage suits a particular retirement plan.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Five hypothetical charts use one gross advance, monthly interest capitalization and an independent annual property-value assumption. Existing-debt settlement and upfront costs reduce initial proceeds. The balance is not capped by property value; no eligibility rule, lending limit, guarantee, current rate or actual legal liability is calculated. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
